title: How to Actually Lead a Team
subtitle: Why leading a ministry team means forming people and not just assigning tasks, and how the difference between managing and leading decides whether your church grows leaders or burns them out.

sections.title: Tasks Are Not People
sections.body:
Most of us learned to lead a team by learning to run a list. We assign, we track, we check the box, we move on. The bulletin gets folded. The chairs get stacked. The slides advance on time. By every measure we know how to read, the team is working.

And the people on it are quietly starving.

I ran teams like this for years before I understood what I was doing. I was not leading anyone. I was deploying them. I treated the people God had given me as a set of hands attached to a calendar, and I called it stewardship because the work got done. The work always got done. That was the problem. It hid what was not happening underneath it.

A team is not a mechanism for completing tasks. A team is a group of souls God has placed in proximity to each other and to you, and the tasks are the occasion, not the point. The early church did not gather to execute deliverables. It gathered, and out of the gathering the work came. Reverse that order and you can build something efficient that forms no one and lasts no longer than your energy holds out.

sections.title: The Difference You Can Feel
sections.body:
Managing asks one question: did the thing get done. Leading asks a harder one: who is the person becoming as they do it.

A manager hands a volunteer a job and measures the job. A leader hands a volunteer a job and watches the person, because the job is a workshop and the person is the work. The same Sunday morning produces two completely different harvests depending on which question you are asking. One produces a folded bulletin. The other produces someone who, two years from now, leads a team of their own.

Jesus had a movement to launch and three years to launch it. He spent most of that time on twelve men. He could have multiplied bread for crowds every afternoon and built the largest following in Galilee. Instead he poured himself into a small group of slow, frightened, ambitious men who kept missing the point. He was not being inefficient. He was leading. He understood that the kingdom does not advance through tasks completed. It advances through people changed.

Managing is necessary. Things must get done, and a leader who cannot manage will drown. But managing is the floor, not the ceiling. The leader who only manages has mistaken the scaffolding for the building.

sections.title: What Forming People Requires
sections.body:
Forming people costs what managing tasks does not. It costs your time when there is no task to justify the meeting. It costs the conversation that has nothing to do with this week's schedule and everything to do with how someone is actually doing. It costs the patience to let someone fail at something you could have done faster yourself.

That last one is where most of us quit. We delegate, the person stumbles, and we snatch the work back because the standard matters and the deadline is real. We tell ourselves we are protecting the ministry. We are protecting our comfort. We would rather carry the load alone than endure the slow, expensive process of watching someone learn.

Paul did not lead Timothy by handing him a task list. He gave him churches that were genuinely his to lead, with genuine authority to fail, and then he wrote him letters that were equal parts instruction and love. Entrust to faithful men who will be able to teach others. That is not a management strategy. That is a man pouring his life into people so that the work would outlive him.

Forming people means you measure your leadership not by what you accomplished this month but by who can do without you next year.

sections.title: Lead From Among, Not Above
sections.body:
There is a kind of leader who stands over a team and a kind who sits among one. The congregation can tell the difference in about a week, and so can the team.

The leader who stands above protects his distance. He keeps the team at arm's length because closeness is risky and information flows up but warmth does not flow down. He is respected and slightly feared and entirely alone, and his team gives him exactly what he asks for and not one ounce more.

The leader who sits among his people has decided that being known is worth the cost of being known. He lets the team see him think, see him reconsider, see him admit he was wrong about the thing he was sure of last month. This is not weakness. It is the only soil in which trust grows. A team will follow a leader off a cliff if they believe he is in the trench with them. They will not cross the street for a leader who manages them from the balcony.

The foot washing was not a teaching illustration. It was a demonstration of where leadership actually comes from. The towel, not the title.

sections.title: The Real Scoreboard
sections.body:
Here is the test, and it is uncomfortable. Walk away from your team for a month. Not a vacation you orchestrated down to the hour. A real absence, unplanned, the kind a hospital stay forces on you. Then come back and look at what you find.

If the ministry collapsed, you were never leading a team. You were the team, and the others were tools you held. You built something that depended on your presence, which means you built something that ends when you do.

If the ministry held, and people you formed made decisions you would have made and a few you would not have, and the work went on without your hand on every piece of it, then you led. You formed people who can stand. That is the only scoreboard that survives you.

The task gets done and is forgotten by Tuesday. The person you formed carries it for thirty years and forms someone else. Lead the person. The tasks will keep. The people will not wait forever for you to notice them.
